title: NGC 4163
caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy NGC 4163, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4163 · constellation Canes Venatici · about 10 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, J. Dalcanton and B. Williams (University of Washington)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A swarm of young, blue stars fills this Hubble view of NGC 4163, a diffuse dwarf irregular galaxy. It belongs to a group of dwarf galaxies that lie near our Milky Way, and it is located roughly 10 million light-years away, in the constellation of Canes Venatici.

Dwarf irregular galaxies are small galaxies without a clear shape. They have no neat spiral arms and no smooth, rounded form like an elliptical galaxy. Instead, their stars are spread in a loose, uneven way, which is why this one looks so diffuse.

Blue stars are usually young and hot, so a crowd of them points to fairly recent star formation within the galaxy. At roughly 10 million light-years, NGC 4163 counts as a close neighbor by astronomical standards.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.27 x 1.56 arcminutes) and distance (10 million light years), the frame spans roughly 9,500 × 4,500 light-years. Its light set out about 10 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters at 475, 606 and 814 nm, in visible and near-infrared light. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble resolves individual stars in this galaxy that would blend into a faint haze without it.
